byId.pr-ussf432: This is SpaceX’s official page for USSF-432, a Falcon 9 mission from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. Company posts show liftoff on 7 Nov 2026 and a first-stage landing on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship; the webpage itself is a JavaScript launch page and returned no extra article text here.
byId.pr-gofororbit: SpaceX released “Go For Orbit,” a recap of the first orbital Starship flight to carry advanced Starlink V3 satellites — the company’s first revenue-generating Starship mission. Official posts describe more than a dozen prior flight tests and years of development; the public page is a JavaScript experience and did not return a long-form transcript here.
byId.pr-q3: SpaceX’s official third-quarter 2026 release reports revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from $5.6 billion a year earlier, with net income of $4.4 billion and Adjusted EBITDA of $8.8 billion. Super Intelligence revenue was $7.56 billion and Connectivity $5.25 billion, with 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers and $69 monthly ARPU; the company also completed its first revenue Starship mission, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites.
byId.pr-cursor: An 8-K says SpaceX closed its acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor) on 14 Aug 2026, converting outstanding Cursor stock into 389,289,254 SpaceX Class A shares at an implied $60 billion equity value, plus 1,752,426 shares for vested RSUs before tax withholding. Unvested Cursor awards were assumed as about 29.1 million SpaceX RSUs and 44.4 million options, and the merger shares were issued in an unregistered Section 4(a)(2) transaction.
byId.pr-q2: SpaceX’s official second-quarter 2026 release reports revenue of $7.8 billion, up 92% from $4.1 billion, a net loss of $541 million, and Adjusted EBITDA of $3.5 billion. The letter highlights two Starship V3 flight tests in 90 days, $14.1 billion of contracted cloud-services sales, the announced $60 billion Cursor deal, 12.0 million Starlink consumer subscribers at $66 ARPU, $47.5 billion of backlog, and $100 billion of cash and marketable securities after the IPO.
byId.pr-ipo-close: SpaceX’s IR release says the IPO closed on 15 Jun 2026 with 638,888,888 Class A shares issued, including the full underwriters’ option for 83,333,333 extra shares, for about $85.7 billion of gross proceeds. Class A shares had begun trading on 12 Jun 2026 on the Nasdaq Global Select Market and Nasdaq Texas under the ticker SPCX.
byId.pr-ipo-price: SpaceX priced 555,555,555 Class A shares at $135.00 and granted the underwriters a 30-day option to buy up to 83,333,333 more shares at the same price. The IR release said trading was expected to start on 12 Jun 2026 on Nasdaq Global Select and Nasdaq Texas under SPCX, with closing slated for 15 Jun 2026.
byId.pr-ipo-launch: SpaceX launched the IPO roadshow for 555,555,555 Class A shares, with an expected $135.00 offer price and the intended ticker SPCX on Nasdaq Global Select and Nasdaq Texas. The company also planned to grant underwriters a 30-day option for up to 83,333,333 additional shares.
byId.filing-0001628280-26-071689: The 8-K reports that Donald Harrison, a Class B director, resigned from the SpaceX board effective 4 Nov 2026, and that the resignation was not because of any disagreement on operations, policies, or practices. An IR note the same day thanks Harrison, who had served since February 2015 and is President of Global Partnerships and Corporate Development at Google.
byId.filing-0001104659-26-118614: The 8-K says that on 24 Oct 2026 SpaceX signed a binding commitment for a master finance lease with an Apollo-managed lessor that will buy GPU pods and related equipment and lease them to SpaceX. The company expects about $40 billion of principal payments over roughly five-year tranche schedules, with closing targeted by year-end 2026 and deliveries in the first half of 2027; an IR release adds that the chips are next-generation NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and that Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and KKR also committed.
byId.filing-0001628280-26-066903: SpaceX filed a Form S-8 with a reoffer prospectus so shares issued in the Cursor acquisition can be resold by employees and other service providers, subject to Rule 144 and any lock-ups. The live EDGAR document could not be fetched here (403); contemporaneous descriptions of this filing put the registered reoffer amount at about 23.6 million Class A shares.
byId.filing-0001628280-26-066880: This is SpaceX’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2026, the full quarterly report that accompanies the Q3 earnings release (revenue $14.6 billion, net income $4.4 billion, Adjusted EBITDA $8.8 billion). The live EDGAR HTML could not be fetched from this environment (403).
byId.filing-0001628280-26-066482: This 8-K furnishes SpaceX’s official third-quarter 2026 earnings release as Exhibit 99.1 under Item 2.02. The exhibit is the same release summarised in the press item: revenue of $14.6 billion (up 161%), net income of $4.4 billion, and Adjusted EBITDA of $8.8 billion.
byId.filing-0001628280-26-056945: This 8-K (Items 2.01 and 3.02) reports that SpaceX completed the Anysphere/Cursor merger on 14 Aug 2026 and issued unregistered Class A shares as merger consideration. Cursor stock converted into 389,289,254 SpaceX shares at an implied $60 billion equity value, with additional shares and assumed awards for Cursor RSUs and options.
byId.filing-0001628280-26-052535: This is SpaceX’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Jun 2026, the full quarterly report that accompanies the Q2 earnings release (revenue $7.8 billion, up 92%, Adjusted EBITDA $3.5 billion). The live EDGAR HTML could not be fetched from this environment (403).
byId.filing-0001628280-26-052515: This 8-K furnishes SpaceX’s official second-quarter 2026 earnings release, the same document as the Q2 press item. The release reports $7.8 billion of revenue, a $541 million net loss, and $3.5 billion of Adjusted EBITDA.
byId.2120432718639145404: Elon Musk is amplifying Starlink’s Mini 2 launch, calling it portable, fast internet that works wherever Starlink is legal. The linked official Starlink post says Mini 2 adds a quick-swap battery (up to 4.5 hours), USB-C, and built-in Wi-Fi, with preorders open — a consumer-hardware push for the Connectivity business.
byId.2120373176060571883: Brian Wang notes that SPCX is getting equipment to make 100 gigawatts of solar per year, linking to related discussion of the SINGULUS order. That matches SpaceX’s and SINGULUS’s own announcements of a supply contract to scale HJT solar-cell lines for Starmind satellites in Bastrop, Texas.
byId.2120347414901252254: Wang says Musk reposted his video arguing SpaceX is turning “dumb” cell towers into smart edge-inference nodes, in line with Musk’s comment that future traffic will be mostly AI-to-AI. The linked post is Wang’s longer $SPCX “AI carrier” thread; it is commentary, not a company filing.
byId.2120302471210033426: Musk says SpaceX has ordered 100 GW a year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from SINGULUS in Germany “for Starmind to create a sentient sun.” SINGULUS’s own release confirms a supply contract for a turnkey HJT line, with the first line due in the first half of 2027 and a plan to support more than 100 GW of equipment as SpaceX scales satellite production in Bastrop.
byId.2120233719491612940: Wang argues SpaceX is moving to become the first “AI carrier,” pointing to the Qualcomm deal, edge inference at towers, and Starlink Direct-to-Cell and V3 satellites. It is investor commentary tying those already-announced pieces together, not a new official contract.
byId.2120231065394590007: SpaceX says it has signed a major supply contract with SINGULUS for advanced solar-cell manufacturing to support more than 100 GW of equipment as it speeds Starmind satellite production in Bastrop, Texas. That is official confirmation of a large solar-capex step for the satellite/AI-power roadmap.
byId.2120220290219208884: SpaceX says Super Heavy has been moved to the Starbase pad; Booster 22, the first V3 booster planned to return for a catch, was used for a suspended squeeze test at catch height. This is hardware progress toward Flight 15, which official posts were then targeting as early as 13 Nov, pending approval.
byId.2120206875581186293: Starlink introduces Mini 2, a next-generation portable kit with up to 4.5 hours on a quick-swap battery, USB-C charging, built-in Wi-Fi, and a claimed 60-second setup, and says preorders are open. For investors this is a new consumer hardware SKU meant to broaden portable Starlink use.
byId.2120182681229246875: Starlink says it will deliver inflight internet on Slate (flyslate), so passengers can stay connected during the flight. It is another airline-install win for the aviation vertical of Connectivity.
byId.2120154857801937384: Wang reports that SpaceX has rewritten Grok 4.8 in C and C++, calling it a different improvement path from Grok 4.7. The post links to Musk’s own thread about dumping JAX and rewriting the training and inference stack; it is commentary on that engineering shift.
byId.2120102767624880364: Musk says Starlink’s software, built to move huge amounts of data through space and to the ground, is also well suited to training superintelligence. The comment ties the Connectivity stack to the Super Intelligence roadmap rather than announcing a new financial metric.
byId.2120099798078656909: Musk, asked about models, says Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 is “a masterpiece” but that Grok 5 “should exceed” it, perhaps in two or three months, with continued acceleration after that. That is a product-timeline comment from the CEO, not a dated backlog or revenue figure.
byId.2120098433159880790: In a follow-up, Musk says the stack even includes some assembly, that superintelligence will one day write a better stack, and that the current code is “tight.” It continues the same thread about SpaceX rewriting its AI software in-house.
byId.2120097663794483601: Musk says SpaceX writes its own headers and calculates its own time (including leap seconds), and that the new Grok AI/SI training and inference stack comes from that engineering culture. For investors it underlines that Super Intelligence software is being built inside SpaceX, not only bought in.
byId.2120088070443655190: Musk says the team has dumped JAX/SGLang and rewritten the reinforcement-learning and inference stack from scratch in C/C++, that pre-training is done, and that Grok 4.8 is now in RL with evals starting. This is a concrete update on the model-training schedule after a time-consuming rewrite.
byId.2119909709197279420: Musk posts “Gwynne is great,” quoting a Tesla Owners Silicon Valley post, in a show of support for president and COO Gwynne Shotwell. It is a leadership signal rather than an operating update.
byId.2119818965266612643: Starlink says its inflight internet is now live on Brussels Airlines (FlyingBrussels). Another airline customer moving from announcement to service supports the aviation part of Starlink’s enterprise story.
byId.2119093662957060389: SpaceX says Starship is preparing for catch and that Flight 15 is targeting launch as early as Friday 13 Nov, pending regulatory approval. That date, plus the later booster rollout and squeeze test, is the near-term Starship catalyst investors have been watching.
byId.2118953789357281607: SpaceX confirms Falcon 9 has launched the USSF-432 mission to orbit from pad 4E in California. It is official completion of a U.S. national-security launch, not a new commercial contract disclosure.
byId.2118870818021097862: SpaceX posts that Falcon 9’s first stage has landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship after USSF-432. A successful landing keeps the usual reusable-launch cadence intact for that mission.
byId.2118868469655433435: SpaceX’s “Liftoff!” post is the USSF-432 Falcon 9 leaving pad 4E at Vandenberg, with video. Together with the later launch-and-landing posts, it documents a completed national-security flight.
byId.2118864998407852102: SpaceX invited viewers to watch Falcon 9 launch USSF-432 from pad 4E, linking a live broadcast. It is a pre-launch watch post for the same mission that later reached orbit.
byId.2118857663106707757: SpaceX said all systems looked good, weather was favorable, and propellant load was about to start for USSF-432 from California. A standard go-for-tanking update ahead of that national-security launch.
byId.2118831607650136119: Starlink is running a fan-ad contest: users can generate a Starlink ad with Grok Imagine and post it on X for a chance to be featured during “the big game,” with details at starlink.com/imagine. It is a marketing campaign tying Starlink to Grok, not an operating result.
byId.2118782721581527457: Starlink says Router 4 is now shipping with Starlink V4 kits in the United States and Canada on Residential 200 Mbps and Residential Max plans. A hardware refresh for higher-tier residential customers, with orders pointed to the residential store.
byId.2118721301300818379: A follow-up to “Go For Orbit” points viewers to the series page on X and to spacex.com/content for every episode and past Starship flight tests. It is a distribution post for the same documentary/recap of the first revenue Starship mission.
byId.2118719281038770389: SpaceX introduces “Go For Orbit,” describing the first orbital Starship launch carrying advanced Starlink satellites after more than a dozen flight tests and years of work. This is the official announcement of the recap that also appears in the press feed.
byId.2118509068897972432: Starlink promotes in-flight gaming on its high-speed, low-latency inflight internet, linking a United post. A marketing example of the airline product rather than a new carrier contract.
byId.2117973275414532165: Starlink says Starlink Mobile will be the first fully integrated U.S. nationwide satellite-and-terrestrial network, and that its 5G base stations will use Qualcomm chips, with deployment starting in 2027. This official post is the company-side announcement of the Qualcomm infrastructure deal also covered in the news feed.
byId.2117713298875654297: Starlink says passengers and crew on Air Tahiti Nui will soon get its inflight internet from gate to gate. Another airline-install announcement for the Connectivity enterprise book.
byId.2116401549828391177: SpaceX confirms a Falcon 9 has launched 27 Starlink satellites from California (the Halloween / group 15-18 mission). A completed rides of the company’s own constellation, supporting the usual launch cadence.
byId.2116396849443598707: SpaceX confirms deployment of those 27 Starlink satellites. The mission has reached the on-orbit step after liftoff and landing.
byId.2116378109218009267: A pre-launch watch post for the same 27-satellite Starlink mission from California. It links a live broadcast ahead of the 31 Oct liftoff.
byId.2116266502533902586: Gwynne Shotwell says she and her husband Robert are giving more than 2 million SpaceX shares, to be distributed in December to children’s Trump accounts, starting with 11-to-17-year-olds in lower-income zip codes, with shares already moving to escrow. The gift is a large personal share transfer, not a company issuance or a change in the official unlock schedule.
byId.2115588901196984822: Starlink Mobile is providing free connectivity to Orange España and Telefónica customers after a train collision in Spain, so people with compatible LTE phones can use apps and texts when towers are down. A disaster-response use case for the direct-to-cell product, not a new rate-plan filing.
byId.2115476295169814978: SpaceX says Ship 42, the Starship for Flight 15, completed a full-duration six-engine static fire and a single-Raptor firing to simulate a deorbit burn. That is a standard pre-flight test milestone on the way to the November attempt.
byId.2115004840321659292: SpaceX confirms another Falcon 9 launch of 27 Starlink satellites from California on 27 Oct. Part of the same high-cadence Starlink launch campaign as the flights around it.
byId.2114998002129440995: Deployment of those 27 Starlink satellites is confirmed. The 27 Oct mission completed satellite release after launch.
byId.2114979142638960965: The watch-party post for the 27 Oct California Starlink launch. A live-broadcast link ahead of liftoff.
byId.2114747196226859108: Starlink says Starlink Mobile is live in Brazil with Vivo, covering the whole country, with 50 million customers able to use apps and messaging in dead zones and 7 million phones already connected. It also teases a next-generation Starlink Mobile V2 service — a sizable emerging-market direct-to-cell launch.
byId.2114695236459094499: Starlink will provide inflight connectivity on easyJet so passengers can work, stream, or stay in touch. A European airline win for the aviation vertical.
byId.2114444137067844004: SpaceX posted a full-duration 33-engine static fire of the Super Heavy booster preparing for Flight 15. A major test of the first-stage engines before the later pad rollout and planned catch attempt.
byId.2113786051009696177: SpaceX confirms a 24 Oct Falcon 9 launch of 27 Starlink satellites from California. Another completed constellation-deployment flight in the late-October cadence.
byId.2113780307904381100: Deployment of those 27 Starlink satellites is confirmed. On-orbit release after the 24 Oct launch.
byId.2113761872264712327: Watch-party post for the 24 Oct California Starlink launch. Live coverage ahead of liftoff.
byId.2113410488319262924: SpaceX stood down from a planned Starlink launch because of unfavorable weather, with the next chance no earlier than 23 Oct. A short delay in the cadence, later followed by the successful 23–24 Oct attempt.
byId.2113400239017378069: The watch post for the Starlink launch that was later stood down for weather on 22 Oct. It shows the attempt was in work before the official delay.
byId.2113365443931148624: SpaceX Super Intelligence says it is proud to be part of an important NVIDIA initiative, quoting an NVIDIA post. A partnership signal for the SI/compute stack, without new contract terms in the post itself.
byId.2112641741937635789: SpaceX posts a link and broadcast for “Q3 2026 Financial and Operational Results.” This is the official pointer to the earnings webcast and the same quarterly release in the press and filings feed.
byId.2112638276389790102: SpaceX’s Q3 highlights post states $14.6 billion of revenue, up 161% year over year, and the first revenue-generating Starship mission, which delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites with about 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. Those figures match the official earnings release.
byId.2112637394654822514: SpaceX says the Q3 2026 earnings report is now public, linking the official PDF, and that a live webcast with Musk, Shotwell, and CFO Bret Johnsen would start in 30 minutes. This is the moment the quarterly results were posted for investors.
byId.2112350370857115965: Starlink says Starlink Mobile has connected more than 11 million people in a year across VEON’s Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Bangladesh markets, often for messaging and location when cell towers cannot reach. A scale update for the direct-to-cell product in those countries.
byId.2111146914121204087: Starlink says it has worked with Indian regulators, industry, and operators for more than five years and has built in-country systems, gateways, and infrastructure so Indian traffic stays in India, “with the requisite government” approvals implied in the truncated post. It is a regulatory-and-infrastructure update on the India market, not a statement that consumer service is already fully live nationwide.
byId.2110416586561433913: SpaceXSI says Grok Voice 3.0 is in the API and Voice Agent Builder at $0.08 per minute and points to a blog with more detail. The official xAI/SpaceXSI post positions it as a priced enterprise voice product.
byId.2110416580899168305: SpaceXSI introduces Grok Voice 3.0 as a speech-to-speech model aimed at customer calls, with sub-second responses and a lower cost than other frontier models. The accompanying blog says it already handles millions of conversations a day at Tesla and SpaceX and is in the API at the prior price.
byId.2110416584183628161: A thread follow-up says Grok Voice 3.0 hits frontier voice-agent performance at 40% lower latency and already resolves 70% of Starlink support calls on its own at SpaceX. That is a concrete cost-and-automation claim for the Connectivity support organisation.
byId.2110410786925641854: Starlink announces that service is now available in Curaçao and links the local order page. A small-market consumer launch that slightly widens the geographic footprint.
byId.2109783337132843366: SpaceXSI says the unified X Subscription covers AI coding in Cursor, work with Grok Bot, Grok chat and creation, and X Premium features. It is the product-bundle follow-up to the plan unification announced in the previous post.
byId.2109783335296008414: SpaceXSI says it has unified plans across Grok, Cursor, and X Premium as “The X Subscription.” A packaging change that ties the consumer AI, coding, and X products together after the Cursor deal.
byId.2108712075371712825: Starlink is giving free service through 10 Nov to new and existing customers in areas of Panama affected by an earthquake, and says it is coordinating with emergency agencies. A disaster-relief offer, not a pricing change in other markets.
byId.2108698771899228179: Starlink Mobile is providing nationwide emergency connectivity to Más Móvil Panama customers so people can stay in touch by SMS, with coverage best under a clear sky. Another emergency direct-to-cell deployment, this time in Panama.
byId.2108681960029831359: Shotwell thanks Brazil’s ANATEL (and its then-head) for approving Starlink Mobile’s priority spectrum rights. It is official cheerleading for the same Brazilian spectrum decision described in the Starlink post.
byId.2108676180467724397: Starlink says ANATEL voted to approve Starlink Mobile’s full 2 GHz access with global S-band priority, which the company says it will use for high-speed mobile broadband in Brazil. A key spectrum approval ahead of the later “now live with Vivo” announcement.
byId.2108302801335918638: Shotwell recaps a launch “triple header” — Starship, Crew-13, and Falcon Heavy — plus a terrestrial low-band spectrum acquisition and FCC approval for the Starlink Mobile constellation, and pride in completing a crew mission. A compact official summary of several operational and regulatory wins from that week.
byId.2108192257967059132: Starlink will put its inflight service across American Airlines’ full mainline fleet so passengers can stream, game, work, and stay in touch. A large U.S. airline fleet win for the aviation vertical.
byId.2107623124909060174: SpaceXSI says Grok 4.7 is live on Microsoft Foundry, with a video. A distribution update putting the model on Microsoft’s cloud marketplace.
byId.2120029978066813318: Starlink says it will bring high-speed, stable internet to SANU (@sanu2ndhome) vacation homes in Japan’s most remote and rural areas, so guests can stream video and make video calls without dropping out. The quoted SANU post says the partnership will add satellite broadband to its new SHELL buildings in places where terrestrial networks barely reach.
byId.2120565589945290827: Musk replies “Much appreciated, Mississippi” to a post reporting that on 10 November Mississippi’s Environmental Quality Permit Board voted to uphold the air permit for SpaceXSI’s permanent Southaven power plant after two days of testimony. That project is described as about 1.2 GW from 41 permanent natural gas turbines to support Super Intelligence compute, including Colossus II.
byId.2120593710107029687: Musk replies that SpaceX is aiming for 1 TW of capacity a year from Earth, rising to over 1 PW a year from the Moon, in response to a post about the company’s 100 GW-per-year solar equipment order. He adds that if that outcome is achieved, SpaceX will “obviously be worth more than Earth, because space is so staggeringly enormous.”
byId.2120592775813255535: Replying to a ZeroHedge post on how much of developers’ data-center pipelines actually gets built, Musk says SpaceX has a chance next year of delivering about half the gigawatts as “actually usable” compute. He stresses that “actually usable” matters, saying it takes SpaceX about two months of 24/7 work to get a large cluster running reliably, and he guesses closer to six months for others.
byId.2120591950961353125: Musk posts two photos captioned “Person for scale,” showing a person in a boom-lift basket beside a towering stainless-steel Starship or Super Heavy cylinder at a high-bay building. The images are a scale check on the vehicle hardware, posted minutes after he highlighted Super Heavy moving to the launch pad.
byId.2120590521253126183: Musk quotes SpaceX’s 10 Nov post that Super Heavy has been moved to the Starbase launch pad, writing “Starship Super Heavy rocket booster moved to launch pad.” The official SpaceX post identified Booster 22 as the first Super Heavy V3 planned to return for a catch and said it was used for a suspended squeeze test at catch height.
byId.2120584928983441826: SpaceX Super Intelligence introduces Grok Bot 1.0, saying bots can be shared and are more collaborative and capable than ever, with a promotional video. The post is the official SI-account launch note for the new teammate product.
byId.2120584703082446863: SpaceX thanks those who have served, including veterans in the SpaceX family, and wishes a happy Veterans Day, with an accompanying image. It is a commemorative company post, not an operational or financial update.
byId.2120584535423565889: Musk urges people to “Hire Grok @Bot as a colleague and give it your hardest tasks,” quoting the official Grok Bot account’s 1.0 launch post. That announcement describes Grok Bots as AI teammates that can be shared, used in Slack and Teams, invited to meetings, and trained to become more helpful.
byId.2120572352073433380: Musk replies that SpaceX would be “happy to take the compute back. No problem,” but that he thinks “the opposite is going to happen,” in a thread about reports that Anthropic told sell-side analysts it may not extend a SpaceX compute contract beyond mid-next year. Those claims about contract size and revenue impact come from other posters in the thread, not from Musk or an official company statement.
byId.2120598044853014716: Starlink posted a Veterans Day customer video featuring Marine veteran John Hassell and nursing student Ashley Hassell, who live on five acres about an hour southwest of Oklahoma City. They say they use the service for VA telehealth, Ashley’s online nursing degree, streaming, gaming and family video calls, and that coverage held up during recent tornado warnings; it is a marketing testimonial, not a new product or plan announcement.
byId.2120622830585024813: Brian Wang notes that SPCX has received a 1.2 gigawatt air permit in Mississippi, quoting an XFreeze post about the same decision. That post says Mississippi’s Environmental Quality Permit Board voted on 10 November to uphold the air permit for SpaceXSI’s permanent Southaven power plant after two days of testimony.
byId.2120621835532534016: Brian Wang writes that Tesla, and maybe SpaceX, might move their headquarters to Florida, quoting a post that says Governor Ron DeSantis has invited Musk to relocate Tesla’s HQ from Texas. The quoted post is commentary about a political invitation after Democrats won in Texas, not a SpaceX or Tesla announcement that a move is happening.
byId.2120613240707420280: Musk replies that 100 GW in space is roughly equal to 800 GW on Earth, arguing the two are not the same at all. He adds that terrestrial solar must be paired with massive batteries to keep compute running at night and supplemented with combustion or nuclear power in winter.
byId.2120628176275845514: Brian Wang calls Grok Bot 1.0 a massive upgrade for $SPCX, saying the bots now work together, take initiative automatically and continuously improve, quoting an XFreeze post on SpaceXSI’s official 1.0 launch. He lists new multiplayer teammate features (sharing bots, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and video meetings), proactive monitoring and follow-up, team-wide learning, and stronger browser, document and integration tools, arguing the biggest shift is that bots no longer need every task assigned.
byId.2120626361408831661: Brian Wang says SpaceX’s Colossus 2 AI data-center campus has bought new southwest property known as Project Mitchell and is getting approval for more power, which he sees as likely a new AI data center beyond the five already being built or near completion. An accompanying map labels Project Mitchell on the southwest side of a Colossus 2 campus that includes Macrohard buildings, and he adds that SpaceX has started buying nearby southeast homes, which he says would likely reduce power-plant noise issues, after SpaceXSI’s 1.2 GW Mississippi permit win.
byId.pr-ussf627: SpaceX’s official USSF-627 page now confirms that Falcon 9 lifted off at 8:36 p.m. PT on 11 November 2026 from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. It says this was the seventh flight for the first-stage booster, which had previously launched NROL-179, SDA-T1TL-E, SDA-T1TL-A and three Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.
byId.2120758305047904548: Musk writes “Try Grok @Bot,” quoting Greg Isenberg’s post calling Grok Bot the best AI agent orchestrator he has seen. That quoted post points to a YouTube walkthrough titled “Grok Bot: Engineering, Design, Content, Money, Shopping,” and says the setup runs Claude Code for engineering and Paper for design.
byId.2120739813401792913: SpaceX posts that Falcon 9’s first stage has landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship after USSF-627. A successful landing keeps the usual reusable-launch cadence intact for that mission.
byId.2120737709924720659: SpaceX’s “Liftoff!” post is the USSF-627 Falcon 9 leaving pad 4E at Vandenberg, with video. Together with the later launch-and-landing posts, it documents a completed national-security flight.
byId.2120734313738391967: SpaceX invited viewers to watch Falcon 9 launch USSF-627 from pad 4E, linking a live broadcast. It is a pre-launch watch post for the same mission that later reached orbit.
byId.2120725054933635188: SpaceX said all systems looked good, weather was favorable, and propellant load was about to start for USSF-627 from California. A standard go-for-tanking update ahead of that national-security launch.
byId.2120808224324510133: SpaceX posts that Falcon 9 has launched the USSF-627 mission to orbit from pad 4E in California, with photos from the flight. This is the official confirmation that the national-security payload reached orbit, after earlier posts on the same mission covering pre-launch status, liftoff and the first-stage landing on Of Course I Still Love You.
byId.pr-building-the-future: SpaceX’s 12 November 2026 Updates post says it is advancing two supercompute projects — a facility at Starbase in the Rio Grande Valley and a campus in Cochise County, Arizona — that together represent more than $74 billion in planned U.S. investment. It plans more than $24 billion of new supercomputing at Starbase (on top of more than $15 billion already invested there), with the site generating its own power, plus $220 million to expand Brownsville’s water and wastewater capacity by 20 million gallons a day, and a roughly $50 billion Arizona campus expected to support about 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, using dry cooling with no planned industrial groundwater use.
byId.2120912138772369758: Musk posts “SpaceX community benefits,” quoting SpaceX’s thread-opening post about building future infrastructure and sharing those benefits with the communities where the company builds. He is amplifying the same official announcement on the Texas and Arizona supercompute sites and related local investment.
byId.2120912086989426746: SpaceX says it has committed $220 million to expand water and wastewater infrastructure for Brownsville and Cameron County, calling it the largest private contribution to Brownsville’s water future in the city’s history. The longer post text adds that the investment is meant to help secure a reliable, sustainable supply of drinking water for generations to come.
byId.2120911969087607288: SpaceX says development of the Starbase supercompute site is creating an opportunity to address decades of environmental neglect, including unauthorized dumping on portions of the property dating back to the 1960s. It says it is cleaning up accumulated debris such as scrap metal, discarded appliances, old tanks, fiberglass insulation, construction materials and thousands of illegally dumped tires.
byId.2120911785217986739: SpaceX says that from the Rio Grande Valley in Texas to Cochise County, Arizona, it is building more than supercomputers — creating jobs, investing in infrastructure, expanding local tax bases and working with communities. The longer post text links to the company’s Cochise County site page.
byId.2120911599749697879: SpaceX posts that it builds the infrastructure of the future and is committed to making sure the communities where it builds share in the benefits, linking its official Updates page and a video. The post opens a thread about new supercompute sites in Texas and Arizona and the related local investment described on that 12 November Updates item.
byId.2120954275799138696: Brian Wang says he will livestream with James of InvestAnswers at noon PST, under the title “How to Play the AI Spectrum,” and argues SpaceX is moving to become the first AI carrier. He repeats points he says Musk earlier reposted: that today’s cell towers are still mostly dumb radios, the Qualcomm deal is about making them AI-native, edge inference at the tower is like an updated Akamai for AI, and Starlink Direct-to-Cell and V3 sit alongside the terrestrial build.
byId.2120957178148471004: In a follow-up to his InvestAnswers livestream post, Brian Wang says the SpaceX idea is not just satellite-to-phone communications, but mini data centers at or near every cell tower plus a mesh of picocells on Tesla cars with Starlink, on homes and businesses, and at Superchargers. He adds that AI5 chips in various boxes or form factors would act as a first-layer triage for an AI inference network.
byId.2120973987635495384: Brian Wang, quoting Bloomberg’s Ed Ludlow, says an SPCX and Tesla merger could happen in four weeks. Ludlow’s post, citing Bloomberg, says SpaceX-Tesla merger negotiations are progressing, with a deal announcement possible by early December, and that boards and advisers are working through terms and governance, with key hurdles including Tesla’s China operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defense ties.
byId.media-40: A Motley Fool article by Leo Sun, published at 4:44 p.m. ET on 19 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 22:44 CET that day, gives two reasons to buy SpaceX — Starlink’s expansion to 13.6 million subscribers at the end of the third quarter, now in 164 countries and territories and boosted by an $8 billion purchase of Grain Management’s 800 MHz spectrum, with Connectivity the only GAAP-profitable segment; and plans for 50–100 Starship launches in 2027 that he says could push adjusted EBITDA, still negative in the first nine months of 2026, into the black — while citing Elon Musk’s view that Starlink, Starship and SI could take revenue from an estimated $49 billion this year to $1 trillion by 2030. The reason to wait is the SI segment (X, xAI, Grok, Cursor and other AI assets), which generated $10.9 billion of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 but a $3.8 billion operating loss, as SpaceX plans to roughly double capex from $19.6 billion in the third quarter to $35–40 billion in the fourth, mostly for Nvidia data-center GPUs; Sun argues that with the stock then around $138, near the $135 IPO price, long-term investors who can ride out the volatility might accumulate shares.
byId.media-barchart-nov13: A Barchart column by Ebube Jones, published 12 Nov 2026, tells SPCX holders to mark Friday 13 Nov for Starship Flight 15, when SpaceX plans to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage with the launch tower’s mechanical arms — a first if it succeeds — after Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 Sept and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Jones notes shares have fallen almost 12% over the past month and that SpaceX and Tesla lost about $456 billion in combined market value after the midterms, argues a successful double catch could help the stock bounce back but would not erase valuation or spending concerns, and cites Morgan Stanley’s Adam Jonas at Overweight with a $300 price target plus a 40-analyst “Moderate Buy” consensus averaging $252.05.
byId.2120995147504853416: Starlink says its service enables gaming, live streaming and chat onboard Southwest Airlines, quoting a HeadShotChick post about four people on a Southwest flight to TwitchCon attempting what they call the first live in-air LAN party over Starlink. The quoted post links a Twitch stream and is marked as an ad.
byId.2120994157380739199: Brian Wang posts “It is so beautiful. $SPCX,” quoting Larry Goldberg’s close-up of Starship S42 — with “DON’T PANIC” written beside the ship number — captioned “Ship emerging. Don’t panic.” He attaches a teary “it’s so beautiful” meme alongside that photo.
byId.2120993535046606952: Brian Wang writes “Spacex and Tesla merger talks accelerating,” quoting an @ns123abc post that says talks are speeding up and a deal announcement could come by December or early 2027. The quoted post is a social-media wrap of the same Bloomberg-reported timeline already in the news feed, not a new official confirmation.
byId.2121120295884837183: Elon Musk writes “Give Grok @Bot your most laborious tasks!,” quoting Maye Musk’s post that she asked Grok Bot the best way to move 2,000 Dropbox Camera Uploads photos into folders and the bot offered to do it, finishing the job in five minutes. byId.2121044579470233638: SpaceX says Ship 42 has moved to the Starbase pad ahead of launch, posting photos of the black-tiled Starship — marked “DON’T PANIC” beside the S42 identifier — being rolled along the coastal road and then standing beside Super Heavy at the catch tower. byId.2121123425213399408: Elon Musk writes “Grok Bot,” quoting the official Grok Bot account’s post that Grok Bot on Mac can now use Messages, Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Location, and Contacts. byId.2121054897584079008: Brian Wang, replying to a comment on his earlier post that a SpaceX–Tesla merger could happen in four weeks, says that timeline is for the announcement of the deal. He adds that actual shareholder votes and execution would take months.
byId.2121250205806772283: Elon Musk writes “Starship 42 preparing for launch,” quoting SpaceX’s post that Ship 42 has moved to the Starbase pad ahead of launch, with photos of the black-tiled Starship being rolled out and standing beside Super Heavy at the catch tower. The quote underscores that Flight 15’s upper stage is at the pad with the booster already in place.
byId.2121242367684661286: Elon Musk writes “Grok is a straight shooter,” quoting Sundar Pichai’s “Nice summary @grok !,” which itself quotes Grok’s reply that cost efficiency decides usage at scale, with Gemini 4 Hydrogen leading on price and speed while Carbon still leads on hard-task capability. The exchange is about Grok’s model-comparison commentary, not a SpaceX operational or financial update.
byId.2121268692453343344: Elon Musk writes “And remember …,” posting a close-up of Ship 42 with “DON’T PANIC” painted beside the S42 identifier and a forward flap extended against the sky. byId.2121267716023546027: Elon Musk writes “Starlink,” quoting Sawyer Merritt’s post of United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby saying in a new interview that Wi-Fi is the No. 1 reason people pick an airline flight and that Starlink is the biggest near-term competitive advantage in United’s 100-year history. Kirby said the service is causing customers to try United because they want Starlink.
byId.2121280048871473281: SpaceX says Boca Chica Beach is not for sale and that the company is not attempting to buy it, adding that the beach is an important part of the Rio Grande Valley community and that SpaceX is investing substantial resources to preserve and improve it. byId.2121317331179614676: Elon Musk writes “Made on Earth by humans,” quoting Andrew McCarthy’s video captioned “Looks like a scene from a sci-fi film but it’s just my drive to work this morning.” The clip, filmed from a roadside at Starbase, shows a fully stacked Starship standing beside the catch tower in morning light, with a canal, cyclists and pedestrians in the foreground.
byId.2121316611974185273: Elon Musk writes “About 4 hours to Flight 15,” quoting SpaceX’s post that links the official Starship Flight 15 livestream. The quote, posted at 19:57 CET on 13 November 2026, indicated the test was then about four hours away.
byId.2121316300702056595: SpaceX posted “Watch Starship Flight 15,” linking to the company’s live X broadcast of the same name. The post is the official stream for Flight 15, shared at 19:56 CET on 13 November 2026, in the hours before the test.
byId.2121323469002437065: Elon Musk writes “Try Grok @Bot,” quoting Anatoli Kopadze’s post calling Grok Bot remarkable for “building a second brain,” and saying a prompt can turn everything you read, watch and think into a knowledge base that organizes itself, with a fuller Grok Bot guide linked below. byId.2121335897744372073: Elon Musk writes “Try Grok @Bot today!,” quoting the official @bot account’s post that Grok Bot can now join meetings, where it can be asked questions, assigned work, or used to keep track of what a team decides. byId.pr-restoring-boca-chica-beach: SpaceX’s 13 November Updates post, titled “Restoring Boca Chica Beach,” says the company has discussed buying about 1,200 acres of Texas Parks and Wildlife land surrounding the Starbase launch facility, with more than half to be permanently protected under a conservation easement, and states clearly that Boca Chica Beach is not part of the proposal and will remain public. It argues the land is largely mudflats and fragile dunes with limited recreation, that securing the perimeter would improve public safety around the launch site, and that sale proceeds would let Texas invest in new parkland in the Rio Grande Valley, while SpaceX commits to permanently conserve about 600 acres and continues beach cleanups and sea-turtle work.
byId.2121361977721106881: SpaceX posted that the live webcast of Starship’s 15th flight test “starts now,” linking to the same official X broadcast as its earlier Flight 15 watch post. byId.2121360601377374680: SpaceX announced “Go for propellant load,” saying teams will soon begin loading Starship with about 12 million pounds of liquid oxygen and liquid methane. byId.2121358365725213183: SpaceX said it is on track for Starship’s 15th flight, with the 75-minute launch window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT on 13 November 2026. byId.2121479482582441991: SpaceX said Starship and its heatshield are healthy as the vehicle continues to orbit Earth after a “spectacular start” nearly seven hours earlier, and that teams are still monitoring systems. byId.2121437515819159871: SpaceX posted a recap clip titled “Liftoff of Starship Flight 15,” showing the Friday evening launch from Starbase. The post went out at 03:58 CET on 14 November 2026, after the vehicle had already reached orbit.

byId.2121376821635936710: SpaceX said Starship’s ascent burn was complete and that the vehicle was on a planned suborbital trajectory while teams checked systems before confirming a proceed-to-orbit decision. The update was posted at 23:57 CET on 13 November 2026.

byId.2121369904469418085: During the Flight 15 webcast, SpaceX invited viewers to look inside its Starlink manufacturing facility in Redmond, Washington, and to watch the latest episode of the Starship docuseries “Go for Orbit.” The post went out at 23:29 CET on 13 November 2026.
byId.2121369682976579588: SpaceX posted that it is “creating jobs, investing in critical infrastructure, expanding local tax bases, and working alongside communities to build a future that benefits the people who live there,” with a video. byId.2121369056066555956: SpaceX said the heatshield tile that YouTuber MrBeast installed was flying to space on this flight, with a video. The post went out at 23:26 CET on 13 November 2026, shortly before Flight 15 liftoff.
byId.2121367063784833448: SpaceX said returning the Ship safely to Starbase requires a robust heatshield and that teams had spent a lot of time iterating on Starship’s heatshield ahead of this flight’s milestone. The briefing post went out at 23:18 CET on 13 November 2026.
byId.2121365911601131986: SpaceX said recovering the entire launch vehicle is considered the “holy grail of rocketry” and that Flight 15 would attempt to recover both stages of Starship for the first time. The post went out at 23:13 CET on 13 November 2026, just after propellant load began.
byId.2121365600811597840: SpaceX said propellant load was underway for the Flight 15 launch. The update was posted at 23:12 CET on 13 November 2026.
byId.2121388517540716839: Elon Musk posted “Live Starship video from space,” sharing in-orbit footage from Flight 15 (the clip is also on SpaceX’s official account). The post went out at 00:43 CET on 14 November 2026, while Starlink V3 deployment was under way.
byId.2121435466016964934: Starlink quoted SpaceX’s in-orbit webcast post and wrote that Starlink is “enabling real-time video streaming from orbit.” The note went out at 03:50 CET on 14 November 2026.
byId.2121384634760220952: Starlink said Flight 15’s payload “will add up to 26 Terabits of capacity to the constellation,” quoting SpaceX’s post that the 26 Starlink V3 satellites were being deployed. The claim was posted at 00:28 CET on 14 November 2026.
byId.2121410868839944340: Brian Wang (NextBigFuture) highlighted a roughly four-month build time for SpaceX’s “Gun Range” data center, quoting a SemiAnalysis thread. That thread says SpaceX has cut typical 8–12 month build times in half, that MiniHard finished in about five months, that the new Gun Range plot just south of the state line is expected to take about four, and that the Memphis/Mississippi campus is planned to go from 0.4 GW of IT in January to 2.4 GW by year-end 2026; Wang’s quote was posted at 02:12 CET on 14 November 2026.
byId.2121408208589967512: Brian Wang posted photos he described as the remains of Flight 15’s Booster 22 in shallow water, adding that the Ship is in orbit and “hopefully has a good return.” The post went out at 02:01 CET on 14 November 2026; it is Wang’s own account, not an official SpaceX statement.
byId.2121383331883561366: Brian Wang wrote that the Flight 15 Super Heavy booster “imploded just before it landed,” that “the metal crumpled inwards,” and that it was an aborted return. byId.2121382045385625920: Brian Wang said Starship was in orbit and would then deploy satellites, and that the tower had been go for a catch before a booster-return abort. byId.2121378894272233817: Brian Wang wrote that the Flight 15 Super Heavy booster “came in hot” and that “some engines did not relight.” The short update was posted at 00:05 CET on 14 November 2026; it is his contemporaneous commentary, not an official explanation from SpaceX.

byId.2121375788977320036: Brian Wang wrote mid-flight that “so far SpaceX flight looks good” and that the booster was returning for a catch (his post has a typo, “catcg”). byId.2121374280462274969: Brian Wang posted “1 minute to launch” ahead of Starship Flight 15, tagging $SPCX. The note went out at 23:46 CET on 13 November 2026.
byId.2121373778894893415: Brian Wang wrote, three minutes before Flight 15, that “the first fully reusable rocket mission could start.” The post went out at 23:44 CET on 13 November 2026, previewing SpaceX’s planned first attempt to recover both stages.
byId.media-38: A Space.com article by Mike Wall, last updated 20 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 18:47 CET that day, says SpaceX’s 35th Dragon cargo mission (CRS-35) undocked from the International Space Station at 12:05 p.m. EST on 20 November, while the station was flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China, and was due to splash down in the Pacific off California at about 4:55 p.m. EST (21:55 GMT) on Saturday 21 November, with no livestream of reentry or splashdown. It says the capsule launched on 13 October, arrived at the station on 15 October with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies, and is bringing back thousands of pounds of cargo, including a 3D-bioprinted blood-vessel construct used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease.
byId.media-26: The full Wall Street Journal article “SpaceX’s Latest Starship Mission Hits Early Setback” (14 November 2026) could not be fetched because of the paywall, so this summary is from the headline only. It reports an early setback on SpaceX’s latest Starship mission.
byId.media-13: A Motley Fool article by Johnny Rice, dated 13 November 2026 and listed in Google News under Yahoo Finance, says Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47 p.m. ET, reached orbit at 6:13 p.m. ET — only the second time Starship has done so — and began deploying 26 Starlink satellites, while the Super Heavy booster was diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown and burst into flames. Rice notes SpaceX has not shared details of the booster issue, that a catch of the upper stage is scheduled for 4:17 p.m. ET on Saturday only if systems stay healthy, and that the Space segment was just $1.8 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue.
byId.media-4: A PBS NewsHour piece by Marcia Dunn of the Associated Press, published 13 November 2026, says SpaceX’s attempt to recover the entire Starship stack at the pad was thwarted when Super Heavy v3 Booster 22 malfunctioned, automatically aborted, and ended up exploding after being diverted to the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship 42 spacecraft still reached orbit. It says this was the first catch attempt for the upgraded 236-foot booster and that, barring further trouble, the ship will try a first-ever return-from-orbit catch Saturday after about 22 hours and 15 laps at roughly 170 miles (275 kilometers), having prepared to deploy 26 of SpaceX’s most advanced Starlink satellites.
byId.media-14: SpaceX’s official NROL-136 mission page, listed in Google News at 19:59 CET on 21 November 2026, says the company is targeting Sunday, 22 November for a Falcon 9 launch from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, with a 30-minute window opening at 4:16 a.m. PT and a backup at 4:02 a.m. PT on Monday, 23 November. It says this will be the 14th flight for the first-stage booster, which previously launched Sentinel-6B, Twilight, NROL-172, Transporter-17, USSF-259 and eight Starlink missions, and that after stage separation the booster is due to land at Landing Zone 4 at Vandenberg.
byId.media-10: Will Robinson-Smith at Spaceflight Now, in an article dated 21 November 2026, listed in Google News at 17:50 CET that day and updated at 8 a.m. EST on 22 November (14:00 CET), reports that SpaceX launched the NROL-136 mission for the National Reconnaissance Office on Sunday morning, sending an undisclosed number of intelligence-gathering satellites to low Earth orbit from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base — the fourth such proliferated-architecture launch this year and the 15th to date. The article says Falcon 9 first-stage booster B1097, making its 14th flight, lifted off at 4:23 a.m. PST (12:23 UTC), 32 hours, 3 minutes and 21 seconds after the prior USSF launch, smashing the Vandenberg pad turnaround record by more than 23 hours, and that the booster landed at Landing Zone 4 about 7.5 minutes after liftoff, the 38th landing at that site and the 680th Falcon booster landing to date.
byId.media-35: A Motley Fool article by Rick Orford, published at 6:30 a.m. ET on 21 November 2026 and listed in Google News via Yahoo Finance at 12:50 CET that day, says Starship Flight 15’s first catch of the upper stage, followed by the Super Heavy booster aborting its catch and being lost in the Gulf, is a mixed milestone that could strengthen confidence in full reusability while also raising questions about development timelines. Orford sketches three 2030 valuation scenarios: a conservative case of 50% annual revenue growth at an 8× sales multiple implying about $96 a share (roughly a third below the then last close), a base case of 65% growth at 12× implying about $210, and an optimistic case of 80% growth at 15× implying about $372, and stresses these are scenarios, not promises.
byId.media-22: A CNBC report by Lora Kolodny, published 13 November 2026, says Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 4:47 p.m. local time (5:47 p.m. ET) after FAA launch authorization, but SpaceX aborted the plan to catch and reuse the booster and diverted it to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown, where it burst into flames. The upper stage continued to orbit for a planned 14 trips around Earth and a Saturday landing back at Starbase; Kolodny notes the flight also deployed another 26 Starlink V3 satellites, that William Blair analysts said even a failed catch and a delay of a few months would not be that consequential, and that SpaceX faces fresh criticism over Starshield restrictions in Ukraine.

byTitle.Here's How Much a $5,000 Investment in S: The Motley Fool uses Street price targets to sketch what a $5,000 SPCX purchase might be worth by November 2027, citing a CNN-tracked median 12-month target of $245 (about 82% above the 6 Nov close of $134.27) and a low target of $118. It notes that 47 analysts cover the stock, with most rating it a buy, and stresses that targets are not guarantees.
byTitle.SpaceX moves Starship Flight 15 booster: Space.com reports that SpaceX rolled Super Heavy Booster 22 to the Starbase pad for Flight 15, targeted as early as Friday 13 Nov 2026, and ran a suspended “squeeze test” at catch height. The article, drawing on SpaceX’s own post, says the plan is a first-of-its-kind double catch of both the booster and the Ship with the tower’s chopstick arms.
byTitle.SpaceX Sets Date For Critical Starship F: Investor’s Business Daily says SpaceX has set an expected date for Starship Flight 15 and plans to attempt a tower catch of the Ship as well as the booster. The piece, which was only partly readable here beyond the opening, also notes SPCX climbed that day as part of a three-day bounce.
byTitle.Starlink Mini 2 Launches: $999 With Buil: A product write-up on BASENOR describes the new Starlink Mini 2 portable terminal, with preorders opened at $999 including a built-in quick-swap battery and a year of service, plus USB-C charging and built-in Wi-Fi. A 10 Nov update in the same article says SpaceX corrected the official field-of-view figure from 55° to 110° after a listing error.
byTitle.Why SpaceX Could Be the Best Buy-and-Hol: This Yahoo Finance column argues SPCX could be a long-term compounder, leaning on Q3 results of $14.6 billion in revenue (up 161%) and $4.4 billion of net income, plus Starlink’s 13.6 million consumer subscribers. It frames launch, Starlink broadband, and the AI business as the main engines of that decade-long case; it is an opinion piece, not a company forecast.
byTitle.Prediction: Here's How Much SpaceX Will: A Motley Fool author predicts SPCX could finish 2027 around $250, about 65% above the then-current $134, after a $1.77 trillion IPO and a pullback to roughly the $135 offer price. The piece cites Q3 Super Intelligence revenue of $7.56 billion and Connectivity revenue of $5.25 billion with 13.6 million subscribers, while warning that the AI landscape can change quickly.
byTitle.Prediction: This Is Where SpaceX Stock W: Yahoo Finance asks where SPCX might trade by the end of 2027 after a jumpy post-IPO path — a first-day valuation near $2.1 trillion and a later slide of about 17% from the first close. It walks through the Space, Connectivity, and Super Intelligence segments and Musk’s ambitious goals; the 2027 price path is the author’s speculation.
byTitle.BT to hold off Starlink launch until Ukr: The Reuters headline, as carried in an Investing.com reprint of the same wire, is that BT will delay launching its Starlink service until public “noise” over Ukraine dies down, according to CEO Allison Kirkby speaking to the Financial Times. Open coverage of that interview says the product is ready and BT still expects to launch in coming months; the Reuters page itself returned 401 here.
byTitle.Elon Musk Just Gave the Top End of His S: This Yahoo Finance story (also run by The Motley Fool) says Musk told the Baron Investment Conference that year-end 2027 annual recurring revenue is “quite likely” to top $500 billion — his “best guess,” not a promise — and put roughly 2% odds on $1 trillion. It notes even the low end would be five times a $100 billion December 2026 pace he discussed, while the stock was then only a little above the $135 IPO price and about 38% below a $225.64 52-week high.

byTitle.Musk: SpaceX Revenue “Will Drop” If Comp: Yahoo Finance reports that Musk said on X on 8 Nov that SpaceX’s revenue “will drop” if compute becomes “plentiful and cheap,” because the company is renting compute near spot prices. The article ties the comment to an All-In discussion of SpaceX’s reported Anthropic compute contract, which either side can end on 90 days’ notice, and to Street expectations that SpaceX revenue could reach $335 billion in 2028.
byTitle.Prediction: $500 a Month Invested in Spa: This Yahoo Finance column is a hypothetical: what a $500 monthly SPCX purchase from November 2026 to year-end 2030 might be worth, set against a stock then trading below the IPO price despite strong Q3 results. It cites official Q3 figures of $14.6 billion in revenue (up 161%) and $8.8 billion of Adjusted EBITDA; the 2030 ending value is an illustration, not a company forecast.
byTitle.SpaceX, Rocket Lab blast higher as NASA: Yahoo Finance says SpaceX and other space stocks rallied after NASA named eight companies, including SpaceX, as winners of a lunar-delivery programme worth up to $10 billion over 10 years. The article describes an expanded Commercial Lunar Payload Services effort for larger landers, announced at Kennedy Space Center on 7 Nov, and notes awards still have to be won mission by mission.
byTitle.SpaceX now fundamentally an \"infrastruc: Ars Technica quotes SpaceX vice president of launch Kiko Dontchev at the UP.Summit in Florida saying the company is “fundamentally an infrastructure company at this point,” not only a rocket firm, after the rise of Starlink and a push into data and AI. byTitle.Here's What Must Happen for SpaceX Stock: A Yahoo Finance commentary says SPCX was down about 22% from its June IPO and asks what would be needed for a rebound, in light of strong Q3 results but a still-heavy valuation. byTitle.SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provi: CNBC says SpaceX struck a multiyear deal with Qualcomm to build base stations for Starlink Mobile, a planned U.S. cellular service meant to complement the satellite network, with a rollout targeted to begin next year. Financial terms were not disclosed; Qualcomm’s Durga Malladi called it a chance to advance 5G and eventually AI-native 6G, and CNBC notes Starlink already accounted for 36% of SpaceX revenue and 85% of operating profit in Q3.
byTitle.SpaceX inks Qualcomm deal, putting Starl: Yahoo Finance describes the Qualcomm agreement as a step toward making Starlink a fourth major U.S. wireless carrier, pairing satellite coverage with a terrestrial 5G build. It frames the deal as part of SpaceX’s push to add spectrum and partners after its consumer mobile offering had been limited compared with the big phone carriers.
byTitle.Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX T: The New York Times headline is that shares of Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX tumbled after Republican losses in the midterms. byTitle.How to Invest In SpaceX (SPCX) — And How: NerdWallet explains how a retail investor can buy SPCX now that SpaceX is public — and how someone who does not want the stock might still end up with exposure through funds — after the 12 Jun IPO at $135 that raised about $75 billion at a $1.75 trillion opening valuation. byTitle.Starlink - Britannica: This Google News item is Encyclopaedia Britannica’s background entry on Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet constellation. The Britannica page itself could not be fetched here (403 / JavaScript challenge), so no additional encyclopedia text is summarised.

A federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi is letting the case proceed; the suit, filed in April 2026 by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, alleges turbines were run without a required air permit.

The essay traces how Musk and Gwynne Shotwell won NASA and military contracts and then became so central that the balance of leverage changed; it is analysis, not a new contract announcement.

byTitle.8-K — Q2 2026 earnings release: This 8-K furnishes SpaceX’s official second-quarter 2026 earnings release, the same document as the Q2 press item. The release reports $7.8 billion of revenue, a $541 million net loss, and $3.5 billion of Adjusted EBITDA.

The linked post is Wang’s longer $SPCX “AI carrier” thread; it is commentary, not a company filing.
byTitle.SpaceX has ordered 100 GW/year of HJT so: Musk says SpaceX has ordered 100 GW a year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from SINGULUS in Germany “for Starmind to create a sentient sun.” SINGULUS’s own release confirms a supply contract for a turnkey HJT line, with the first line due in the first half of 2027 and a plan to support more than 100 GW of equipment as SpaceX scales satellite production in Bastrop.
byTitle.SpaceX is making moves to become the fir: Wang argues SpaceX is moving to become the first “AI carrier,” pointing to the Qualcomm deal, edge inference at towers, and Starlink Direct-to-Cell and V3 satellites. byTitle.We have signed a major supply contract w: SpaceX says it has signed a major supply contract with SINGULUS for advanced solar-cell manufacturing to support more than 100 GW of equipment as it speeds Starmind satellite production in Bastrop, Texas. byTitle.Starlink is now delivering fast, reliabl: Starlink says its inflight internet is now live on Brussels Airlines (FlyingBrussels). Another airline customer moving from announcement to service supports the aviation part of Starlink’s enterprise story.

byTitle.Watch Falcon 9 launch the USSF-432 missi: SpaceX invited viewers to watch Falcon 9 launch USSF-432 from pad 4E, linking a live broadcast. It is a pre-launch watch post for the same mission that later reached orbit.

byTitle.Game in-flight with Starlink’s high-spee: Starlink promotes in-flight gaming on its high-speed, low-latency inflight internet, linking a United post. A marketing example of the airline product rather than a new carrier contract.

byTitle.SpaceX must face sex-bias claims after a: A Reuters story, consistent with the Ninth Circuit’s 10 Nov 2026 opinion in Holland-Thielen v. SpaceX, says SpaceX must face sex-bias and related claims in court after the appeals court rejected its bid to force the case into arbitration. A 2–1 panel held that the Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act applies; the eight former employees allege they were fired after circulating a letter about conduct they called sexual harassment. The ruling decides the forum, not the merits. Reuters.com itself was paywalled here (401).

Invitations seen on X price it at $999 including a year of Roam Unlimited that SpaceX values at $2,100; the dish is thinner than the original Mini (23.1 mm vs 38.5 mm), a bit heavier at about 3.5 pounds, still IP67-rated, with preorders open by invitation for select US customers and coming soon to more customers and countries.
byTitle.SpaceX, Rocket Lab blast higher as NASA: Yahoo Finance says SpaceX and other space stocks rallied after NASA named eight companies, including SpaceX, as winners of a lunar-delivery programme worth up to $10 billion over 10 years. byTitle.What time will SpaceX launch Starship Fl: Space.com reports that Starship Flight 15 is targeted no earlier than Friday 13 Nov 2026 at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) from Starbase, in a 75-minute window through 7 p.m. EST, as SpaceX’s first attempt to catch both Super Heavy Booster 22 (about 6.5 minutes after liftoff) and Ship after a roughly 22.5-hour, 14-orbit flight. byTitle.SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper st: A Space.com article by Mike Wall, published 21 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 14:00 CET that day, says Elon Musk told the TomorrowX Summit on Wednesday, 18 November, that Ship 42 — the first Starship upper stage SpaceX ever successfully recovered, caught at the Starbase tower after Flight 15 — will not fly again and will instead be left for public display because it is “kind of an historic ship,” even though he said it “could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment.” Wall writes that Musk did not say where the ship would be put on display, notes that SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy three times and reflown a booster twice but had never before attempted a Ship catch, and recalls Musk’s target of about 10,000 Starship missions a year by 2030.
byTitle.Trump intel chief warned no funding for: The CNN.com article itself could not be fetched here; this summary is from the CNN-bylined report by Zachary Cohen, Jennifer Hansler and Kylie Atwood, carried by KRDO and RNZ and listed in Google News at 19:09 CET on 20 November 2026. byTitle.SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule heads home t: A Space.com article by Mike Wall, last updated 20 November 2026 and listed in Google News at 18:47 CET that day, says SpaceX’s 35th Dragon cargo mission (CRS-35) undocked from the International Space Station at 12:05 p.m. EST on 20 November, while the station was flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China, and was due to splash down in the Pacific off California at about 4:55 p.m. EST (21:55 GMT) on Saturday 21 November, with no livestream of reentry or splashdown. byTitle.Live coverage: SpaceX to launch intellig: Will Robinson-Smith at Spaceflight Now, in an article dated 21 November 2026, listed in Google News at 17:50 CET that day and updated at 8 a.m. EST on 22 November (14:00 CET), reports that SpaceX launched the NROL-136 mission for the National Reconnaissance Office on Sunday morning, sending an undisclosed number of intelligence-gathering satellites to low Earth orbit from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base — the fourth such proliferated-architecture launch this year and the 15th to date.
